## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.65590.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.65590.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Acceptance summary:

A key step towards understanding the cortical representation of color is to develop mathematical models that accurately and parsimoniously describe cortical representations of broad families of colorful stimuli. This study achieves this goal with the quadratic color model, a new benchmark f-or the quantitative assessment of cortical light responses that provides new insights into the underlying mechanisms.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "A Quadratic Model Captures the Human V1 Response to Variations in Chromatic Direction and Contrast" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Gregory D Horwitz as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Tirin Moore as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Stephen A Engel (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

(1) The paper would be strengthened by a more thorough analysis of the QCM: comparison of the QCM to models more biologically plausible than the GLM, residuals analyzed for meaningful patterns, and quality-of-fit metrics compared with those of previous studies.

(2) The new results should be discussed in the context of previous EEG and fMRI studies.

(3) Trends in the data should be compared with predictions from psychophysics.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The quality of QCM fits could be appraised more rigorously. Are there any consistent patterns in the residuals? If so, what is the nature of the systematic deviations from the QCM, how big are they, and what might they indicate about the underlying biology?

The GLM allows jagged and non-monotonic contrast-response functions, which is unrealistic. A more useful benchmark would be a model in which contrast-response functions have a Naka-Rushton form, like they do in the QCM.

Neurons in the LGN respond more strongly to 12 Hz, full-field modulations than do most neurons in V1. One possibility is that much of the BOLD signal recorded from V1 under the conditions used in this study reflects the activity of LGN afferents. Some comments on this and potential consequences for the activation of V1 and beyond would be useful.

The changes in minor axis ratio and ellipse orientation with eccentricity are modest, but it is unclear how large we should expect them to be. Predictions from psychophysics, neurophysiology, or anatomy would provide a more useful benchmark than estimates of measurement error ("vertical spread of values at each eccentricity" and "set-to-set differences in parameters values").

More information should be giving regarding the bootstrap calculation of the 68% confidence intervals. Was the percentile method used? Was a normal distribution of parameter estimates assumed ({plus minus}1 SD of bootstrap resamples)?

Line 171: The measured BOLD percent signal change is described as "black line" in the text but more accurately as "thin gray line" in the figure legend.

Lines 626 and 627: Is an experimental run distinct from a functional run?

The discussions of cone fundamentals changing with eccentricity and contrast-response functions changing with eccentricity might be easier to understand if they were separated (both are described in the paragraph spanning lines 422-459).

The legends to Figure 12 and Supplementary Figure 9 are missing at least one line of text.

Typos: "Varience", "grayoordinate", "2-dimentional", "…and the bottom set of the show data for…"

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This paper presents an important data set and model, and the successes of the paper are laid out in the other portions of this review process. Here I detail specific concerns that could be addressed in revision. Larger ones fall into four categories

1. Response patterns could be characterized even more completely, aiding readers.

Line 175: How does this R2 of the GLM compare to those reported in prior work? It would be good to know if it is in the standard range, which I bet it is.

Figure 2: Potting more of the results in terms of percent signal change rather than arbitrary units would allow comparison with previous results. This might also help readers interpret the lack of saturation of response as a function of contrast.

Line 281: It would be good to give readers a better sense of what responses are like outside of V1. Specifically, what quantitative estimates are there to support the claim that the stimuli are not driving activity beyond V1, even in V4 or V01? One solution might be to show a map of GLM variance explained throughout cortex, with some sample timecourses shown for V4ish and V01ish ROIs. It also may not be clear to non-specialists that neurons beyond V1 require spatial contrast to drive response; this could probably be highlighted more.

2. Additional comparisons of GLM and QCM.

General: While agreement between GLM and QCM is good, are there small but systematic differences? It might be helpful to include some sort of plot of residuals of the QCM fits. I think that is part of the point of Figure 7, but one could plot residuals explicitly, and it is not clear from the figure (at least to me) whether this plot is evaluating fits of just the contrast non-linearity or the entire QCM model. Figure 8: Another additional analysis that might be useful is a spatial map of a GLM to QCM comparison. It seems possible, at least in principle, that there are parts of the brain where the difference between the two models could be larger than in V1.

3. Discussion of other work.

While this is generally quite thorough, the manuscript would be strengthened by discussing the two additions mentioned in the public review: EEG results (e.g.Baseler and Sutter), and Brouwer and Heeger's "channel" model of color responses in cortex.

4. Discussion of implications for neurons in V1. A few additions to the discussion might be helpful. First, could the present results be dominated by input to V1 rather than action potentials generated within V1? This merits some discussion. Relatedly, readers might like to know if the present data set covered the LGN, which could be used in future work to address this issue.

Second, as mentioned above, additional discussion of what single unit work says about what kind of neurons will give strong responses to spatially uniform stimuli, and where they are located in cortex, could be useful.

Finally, and most trickily I suppose, is what conclusions about neurons can one make from the good QCM fit itself (besides lack of eccentricity effects). Can one conclude that for these stimulus conditions neurons in V1 whose preferred color direction is at or near L-M have higher gain than neurons whose preferred color direction is at or near L+M? I realize that there are a lot of assumptions (e.g. about separability and pooling of the signals by the fMRI response) being made in such a statement. I guess one could also build an "LGN-type" model that assumes all signal comes from just L+M or L-M tuned neurons, which could fit comparably to the QCM, but potentially with fewer parameters, since it assumes a 45 degree orientation of one population and a 135 degree orientation of another (almost equivalently a 2 channel version of the Brouwer and Heeger model). This is hinted at in line 370 in terms of psychophysics, but the model can be constrained by single unit data, at least from LGN. Is there anything useful one could conclude from such fits?

A final possible form this discussion could take is to tackle the question: Are there plausible neural response patterns that would be expected to not be well-fit by the QCM, and so the present data discomfirm them? I understand the authors' desire to not be speculative, but readers may already be speculating.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

I think the main weakness here is the link between biology and data. Is it possible to implement a simple but biologically plausible population model of color processing in V1 (involving just the low SF-sensitive neurons) and test it against the data here? Such a model might have more than 6 parameters.… but fewer than 40: as the authors point out, the data are consistent with a model that sums approximately independent inputs from L-M and L+M channels. The authors might then discuss (qualitatively) how they expect the response functions to change as other populations of chromatically-sensitive neurons are excited by, for example, the presence of spatial structure.

Psychophysical data would also benefit the paper. I know there would be a lot of conditions – but with efficient staircases, data could be collected on at least some subjects to examine, for example, the observation that model parameters do not change across eccentricity (a surprising and interesting result!). Absent that, some more quantitative comparisons with existing psychophysical data (and neuroimaging data – for example Brouwer and Heeger's work) would be nice.

claims.claim: Psychophysical evidence supports the existence of two cone-opponent mechanisms (S-(L+M) and L-M) and a luminance mechanism (L+M).

claims.evidence: Supported by citations to psychophysical literature (Krauskopf et al., 1982; Stockman and Brainard, 2010).

claims.claim: Physiological evidence shows that cone signal recombination begins in the retina with correlates observed in retinal ganglion cells and lateral geniculate nucleus neurons.

claims.evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies (De Valois et al., 1966; Derrington et al., 1984; Lennie and Movshon, 2005).

claims.claim: Studies have not yet converged on a widely accepted quantitative parametric model of chromatic response properties of neurons in primate primary visual cortex (V1).

claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing lack of consensus (Johnson et al., 2004; Solomon and Lennie, 2005; Tailby et al., 2008; Horwitz and Hass, 2012; Weller and Horwitz, 2018).

claims.claim: Considerable heterogeneity of chromatic response properties exists across individual cortical neurons in V1.
claims.source: In part, this is due to the considerable heterogeneity of chromatic response properties found across individual cortical neurons (Gegenfurtner, 2001; Lennie and Movshon, 2005; Solomon and Lennie, 2007; Shapley and Hawken, 2011; Horwitz, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies documenting heterogeneity (Gegenfurtner, 2001; Lennie and Movshon, 2005; Solomon and Lennie, 2007; Shapley and Hawken, 2011; Horwitz, 2020).

claims.claim: The QCM was fit to data using the MATLAB function fmincon to minimize the root mean squared error between the actual fMRI time course and the QCM prediction.

The data were fit using the MATLAB function fmincon to find a set of model parameters that minimize the difference between the actual fMRI time course and the QCM prediction of the time course, computed as the root mean squared error.
claims.evidence: This is a direct description of the model fitting procedure.

claims.claim: All code used to perform analyses is publicly available in a GitHub repository.
claims.source: All code used to perform analyses in this paper may be found in our public GitHub repository: https://github.com/BrainardLab/LFContrastAnalysis_eLife.git (copy archived at swh:1:rev:c9b4cbe72e69e4d3d623ec8b7fc62076e2fe1a22, Barnett, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of code availability.

claims.claim: Engel et al., 1997 found that for low temporal frequencies the psychophysical isothreshold and BOLD fMRI isoresponse contours in the LM contrast plane were well-described as ellipses and had similar shapes.
claims.source: For example, an approach to studying chromatic sensitivity is to characterize the isothreshold contour, which specifies the set of stimulus modulations that are equally detectable. Engel et al., 1997 took this approach and found that for low temporal frequencies the psychophysical isothreshold and BOLD fMRI isoresponse contours in the LM contrast plane were well-described as ellipses and had similar shapes.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Engel et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Psychophysical isothreshold contours remain well-described by ellipses at higher temporal frequencies, but their orientation changes to favor L+M sensitivity over L-M sensitivity.
claims.source: As they note, although psychophysical isothreshold contours remain well-described by ellipses at higher temporal frequencies, their orientation changes to favor L+M sensitivity over L-M sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Engel et al., 1997 and related literature.

claims.claim: A quadratic isoresponse contour can be produced by a quadratic mechanism that computes a sum of the squared responses of two underlying linear mechanisms.
claims.source: More generally, a quadratic isorepsonse contour can be produced by a quadratic mechanism that computes a sum of the squared responses of two underlying linear mechanisms, where the output of each linear mechanism is a weighted sum of L- and M-cone contrasts (Poirson et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical explanation with citation to Poirson et al., 1990.

claims.claim: The isoresponse contours do not uniquely determine the sensitivity of the underlying linear mechanisms, even within the QCM together with the assumption that there are two such mechanisms.
claims.source: Note, however, that other pairs of underlying mechanisms are also consistent with the same elliptical isoresponse contours (Poirson et al., 1990), so that our isoresponse contours do not uniquely determine the sensitivity of the underlying linear mechanisms, even within the QCM together with the assumption that there are two such mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical considerations with citation to Poirson et al., 1990.

claims.claim: The Linear Channels Model (LCM) accounts for the data about as well as the QCM.
claims.source: To illustrate this point, we developed and fit an alternate model, the Linear Channels Model (LCM), a variation on the Brouwer and Heeger channel model (Brouwer and Heeger, 2009; Kim et al., 2020), that accounts for our data about as well as the QCM (see Appendix 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by cross-validation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The best fitting isoresponse contours found with the LCM approximate the ellipse found using the QCM, but are not perfectly elliptical.
claims.source: The best fitting isoresponse contours found with the LCM, which could in principle deviate considerably from an ellipse, none-the-less approximate the ellipse we found using the QCM, but are not perfectly elliptical (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of isoresponse contours in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A form of the QCM with the angle constrained to 0 degrees resulted in a noticeably lower cross-validated R2 compared to all other models tested.
claims.source: To address this, we fit and cross-validated a form of the QCM with the angle constrained to 0 degrees. This resulted in a noticeably lower cross-validated R2 for this model as compared to all other models we tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, labeled at 'QCM locked')
claims.evidence: Supported by cross-validation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The spatially uniform (0 c.p.d.) chromatic modulations at 12 Hz could drive 'color', 'luminance' and 'color-luminance' cells as described by Johnson et al., 2001, depending on the particular chromatic direction.
claims.source: Our stimuli were large, spatially uniform (effectively 0 c.p.d.) chromatic modulations that were temporally modulated at 12 Hz. These stimuli could drive 'color', 'luminance' and 'color-luminance' cells as described by Johnson et al., 2001, depending on the particular chromatic direction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on stimulus properties and citation to Johnson et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The 0 c.p.d. stimuli would presumably produce strong responses in 'color' cells for the L-M direction, given that these cells are thought to behave as low-pass filters in the spatial domain and have unoriented receptive fields.
claims.source: The 0 c.p.d. stimuli would presumably produce strong responses in the 'color' cells for our L-M direction, given that these cells are thought to behave as low-pass filters in the spatial domain and have unoriented receptive fields.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of color cells.

claims.claim: At 0.1 c.p.d., firing rates for color cells are roughly 5x times higher than the firing rates for luminance and color-luminance cells according to Schluppeck and Engel, 2002.
claims.source: Schluppeck and Engel, 2002 plot the spatial frequency response function estimated from the data from Johnson et al., 2001. These functions plot the average firing rate as a function of spatial frequency for the color, color-luminance, and luminance cells. Taking the lowest spatial frequency present in the dataset (0.1 c.p.d.), firing rates for color cells are roughly 5x times higher than the firing rates for luminance and color-luminance cells.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Schluppeck and Engel, 2002 analyzing data from Johnson et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The average minor axis ratio of approximately 0.2 indicates V1 is roughly five times more sensitive to L-M than to L+M, which is the same as the ratio of firing rates for color cells versus luminance and color-luminance cells at low spatial frequencies.
claims.source: This is the same as our average minor axis ratio which indicates V1 is roughly five times more sensitive to L-M than to L+M.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the QCM results to electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The data do not distinguish the extent to which the response properties of the BOLD signals measured in V1 are inherited from the LGN or are shaped by processing within V1.
claims.source: It is also important to note that our data do not distinguish the extent to which the response properties of the BOLD signals we measure in V1 are inherited from the LGN or are shaped by processing within V1.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the results.

claims.claim: The spatiotemporal properties of the stimuli would robustly drive cells in the LGN that project to V1.
claims.source: The spatiotemporal properties of our stimuli would robustly drive cells in cell in the LGN that project to V1 (Lankheet et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on stimulus properties with citation to Lankheet et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The V1 sensitivities found from fitting the QCM may be inherited from areas prior to V1 or could be affected by feedback from other cortical areas.
claims.source: As such, the V1 sensitivities found from fitting the QCM may be inherited from areas prior to V1. In principle, they could also be affected by feedback from other cortical areas.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about possible sources of the measured responses.

claims.claim: Quadratic models have been used to characterize the isoresponse properties of individual neurons in macaque V1, with roughly half of neurons best fit by quadratic isoresponse surfaces and the other half by linear models.
claims.source: Finally, it is interesting to observe that quadratic models have been used to characterize the isoresponse properties of individual neurons in macaque V1 (Horwitz and Hass, 2012). Roughly half of the neurons tested in this paper were best fit by quadratic isoresponse surfaces (in the L-, M-, and S-cone contrast space) while the other half were well fit by a linear model whose isoresponse surfaces were parallel planes.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Horwitz and Hass, 2012.

claims.claim: Of the quadratic isoresponse surfaces in individual neurons, some were ellipsoidal while others were hyperbolic.
claims.source: Of the quadratic isoresponse surfaces, some were ellipsoidal while others were hyperbolic.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Horwitz and Hass, 2012.

claims.claim: Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 report a decrease in the V1 response to L-M modulations with eccentricity, while the response to L+M remains roughly constant.
claims.source: Both Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 report a decrease in the V1 response to L-M modulations with eccentricity, while the response to L+M remains roughly constant.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The findings of Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 differ from the current study's result of no change in chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
claims.source: This differs from our result, and the size of the effects in these papers are large enough that we would expect that if they were present in our data they would be visible in the analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior findings.

claims.claim: Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 speculate that the mechanism underlying decreased L-M sensitivity with eccentricity is non-selective (random) connections between L and M cones and retinal ganglion cell receptive fields.
claims.source: Both speculate that the mechanism underlying this observation is non-selective (random) connections between L and M cones and retinal ganglion cell receptive fields.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to speculation from Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006.

claims.claim: If connections between cones and ganglion cells are non-selective, L-M sensitivity would be expected to decrease with eccentricity because receptive field pooling area increases with distance from the fovea.
claims.source: If these connections are non-selective, L-M sensitivity would be expected to decrease with eccentricity. This is because the area in which receptive fields pool cone inputs increases with distance from the fovea, progressively reducing the likelihood that random L- and M-cone inputs to the center and surround will produce chromatic opponency (Lennie et al., 1991; Mullen and Kingdom, 1996; Wool et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical explanation with citations to Lennie et al., 1991; Mullen and Kingdom, 1996; Wool et al., 2018.

claims.claim: D'Souza et al., 2016 find, for the majority of spatial frequencies studied, no change in L-M response relative to the response to isochromatic luminance modulations with eccentricity.
claims.source: In contrast, D'Souza et al., 2016 find, for the majority of spatial frequencies studied, no change in L-M response relative to the response to isochromatic luminance modulations.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from D'Souza et al., 2016.

claims.claim: D'Souza et al., 2016 take their result as supporting the idea that connections between cones and some classes of ganglion cells are selective for cone type and preserve chromatic sensitivity across the retina.
claims.source: Following the same line of reasoning as Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 but reaching the opposite conclusion, D'Souza et al., 2016 take their result as supporting the idea that connections between cones and some classes of ganglion cells are selective for cone type and preserve chromatic sensitivity across the retina.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to the interpretation from D'Souza et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density can produce eccentricity-dependent deviations in the degree of actual cone contrast reaching the photoreceptors.
claims.source: One such factor is the changes in cone spectral sensitivity with eccentricity, caused primarily by variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density. Variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density can produce eccentricity-dependent deviations in the degree of actual cone contrast reaching the photoreceptors.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of a potential confound based on known optical properties of the eye.

claims.claim: Prior studies examining eccentricity effects do not account for variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density.
claims.source: Prior studies do not account for this variation, leading to the possibility that effects of eccentricity on sensitivity are due to receptoral, rather than post-receptoral mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a critique of prior studies based on methodological considerations.

claims.claim: In the current study, spectral modulations were designed to produce the same contrasts in both 2-degree and 15-degree cone fundamentals, which reduces the change in cone contrast with eccentricity.
claims.source: In our study, we designed spectral modulations that produce the same contrasts in both 2-degree and 15-degree cone fundamentals (see Materials and methods and Tables 5–7). This reduces the change in cone contrast with eccentricity for our stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a methodological feature of the current study.

claims.claim: The lack of variation in chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity in the data is parsimoniously explained by retinal output that preserves chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
claims.source: Although changes in sensitivity with eccentricity can be caused by mechanisms at many levels of the visual system, the lack of such variation in our data is parsimoniously explained by retinal output that preserves chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: Studies show random or close to random inputs from L- and M-cones to midget ganglion cell centers in the retinal periphery.
claims.source: This interpretation is challenged by studies that show random (Wool et al., 2018) or close to random (Field et al., 2010) inputs from L- and M-cones to midget ganglion cell centers in the retinal periphery.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Wool et al., 2018 and Field et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Not all studies of midget cell chromatic responses or their parvocellular LGN counterparts agree with non-selective wiring.
claims.source: Not all studies of midget cell chromatic responses or their parvocelluar LGN counterparts agree with non-selective wiring (Reid and Shapley, 1992; Martin et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Reid and Shapley, 1992; Martin et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012.

claims.claim: One possible cortical mechanism that could compensate for reduced L-M signal-to-noise ratio with eccentricity is supra-threshold compensation for reduced signals.
claims.source: One possible cortical mechanism that could compensate for the reduced L-M signal-to-noise ratio with eccentricity as predicted by random wiring models is supra-threshold compensation for reduced signals.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claims.claim: Mechanisms of supra-threshold compensation have been postulated in the domain of contrast perception and anomalous trichromatic vision.
claims.source: Mechanisms of this sort have been postulated in the domain of contrast perception (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975) and anomalous trichromatic vision (Boehm et al., 2014; Tregillus et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to prior work on compensation mechanisms (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975; Boehm et al., 2014; Tregillus et al., 2021).

claims.claim: A differential change in stimulus integration area across chromatic directions and with eccentricity is not supported by fMRI population receptive field measurements for modulations in different chromatic directions in V1.
claims.source: Another possibility is a differential change in stimulus integration area across chromatic directions and with eccentricity. However, this latter possibility is not supported by fMRI population receptive field (pRF) measurements for modulations in different chromatic directions in V1 (Welbourne et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to findings from Welbourne et al., 2018 that rule out a particular explanation.

claims.claim: The QCM may be generalized to handle stimuli in the full L-, M-, and S-cone contrast space by replacing the elliptical isoresponse contours with ellipsoidal isoresponse surfaces.
claims.source: In our study, we only measured responses to stimuli confined to the LM contrast plane. A more general account of chromatic contrast sensitivity requires modulating stimuli in all three-dimension of the full L-, M-, and S-cone contrast space. The QCM may be generalized in a straightforward manner to handle this expanded stimulus set by replacing the elliptical isoresponse contours with ellipsoidal isoresponse surfaces, but we have yet to test this generalization.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal for future work based on the current model structure.

claims.claim: The QCM could be readily fit to data from modulations at various temporal frequencies to observe how chromatic sensitivity changes with temporal frequency.
claims.source: Another way in which the QCM may be generalized, even within the LM contrast plane, is to consider modulations at other temporal frequencies. In our experiment, we fixed the temporal modulation of the stimulus at 12 Hz. The QCM could be readily fit to data from modulations at various other temporal frequencies with the goal of observing how the chromatic sensitivity changes.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal for future work.

claims.claim: If the response to temporal frequency mixtures can be predicted via a simple rule of combination, establishing the QCM parameters for a well-chosen set of temporal frequencies would enable prediction of the BOLD response to chromatic stimuli modulated with complex temporal sequences.
claims.source: With this, one could further examine the BOLD response to mixtures of different temporal frequency modulations. This is particularly interesting in that any arbitrary complex temporal modulation can be decomposed into an additive mixture of modulations at different temporal frequencies and phases (Bracewell, 1978). If the response to temporal frequency mixtures can be predicted via a simple rule of combination (such as linearity), establishing the QCM parameters for a well-chosen set of temporal frequencies would enable prediction of the BOLD response to chromatic stimuli modulated with complex temporal sequences.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential generalization of the model with citation to Bracewell, 1978.

claims.claim: Examining how the QCM fits change with changing spatial frequencies might allow for models of the BOLD response to arbitrary complex spatial stimuli.
claims.source: Just as we had a fixed temporal frequency in our experiment, the stimulus presented also had a fixed spatial frequency (0 c.p.d.). Similar to the temporal domain, complex spatial images can be broken down into a combination of oriented two-dimensional sine wave patterns at single spatial frequencies and phases. Examining how the QCM fits change with changing spatial frequencies might allow for models of the BOLD response to arbitrary complex spatial stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential generalization of the model.

claims.claim: Recent work has developed quantitative forward models of the BOLD response of early visual cortex to a variety of achromatic modulations with different spatial patterns.
claims.source: Consistent with this general goal, recent work has developed quantitative forward models of the BOLD response of early visual cortex to a variety of achromatic modulations with different spatial patterns (Kay et al., 2013a; Kay et al., 2013b).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to prior work by Kay et al., 2013a; Kay et al., 2013b.

claims.claim: How forward models of BOLD response should be generalized to handle chromatic modulations is not known.
claims.source: These models have sequential stages of processing that operate on an input image and transform it into a model of the BOLD response. How such models should be generalized to handle chromatic modulations is not known.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claims.claim: If the QCM holds for other spatial frequencies, such a result would place important constraints on the appropriate generalization for forward models to incorporate color.
claims.source: If the QCM holds for other spatial frequencies, such a result would place important constraints on the appropriate generalization for such forward models to incorporate color.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the implications of potential future findings.

results.result: The Quadratic Color Model (QCM) with 6 free parameters explains the same cross-validated variance as a conventional General Linear Model (GLM) with 41 free parameters when modeling V1 BOLD fMRI responses to chromatic modulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C25, and C26 demonstrate that the QCM achieves similar or slightly better cross-validated R² compared to the GLM (Figure 4), despite having far fewer parameters (C12: 6 vs C13: 41). The cross-validation procedure (C88-C90) properly accounts for model complexity, making this a fair comparison. The replication across measurement sets strengthens this finding.

results.result: The QCM generalizes to predict V1 responses to untested chromatic directions through leave-session-out cross-validation, with better generalization from Session 1 to Session 2 than vice versa, likely due to Session 1 including directions that better constrain model parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C27 are supported by leave-session-out cross-validation results (C91-C92) shown in Figure 5 and supplements. The asymmetric generalization performance (C28) is explained by the experimental design (C29), where Session 1 includes chromatic directions near the major axis of the ellipse. This demonstrates both the model's generalization capability and its sensitivity to stimulus sampling.

results.result: Results replicate well across two independent measurement sets for each of three subjects, demonstrating reliability of the findings.
results.evaluation: Claim C3 is supported by consistent results across Measurement Sets 1 and 2 (C20) shown throughout Figures 2, 6, 7, and other results sections. The replication design with randomized stimulus orders across measurement sets provides strong evidence for reliability. Agreement is demonstrated both within and across subjects.

results.result: Within the LM cone contrast plane, V1 is most sensitive to L-M contrast modulations and least sensitive to L+M modulations, with approximately 5-fold difference in sensitivity as indicated by elliptical isoresponse contours oriented at ~45° with minor axis ratios of 0.15-0.25.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 are supported by the QCM isoresponse contours (Figure 6) showing consistent ellipse angles of ~45° (C14) across all subjects and measurement sets. The minor axis ratios of 0.15-0.25 (C16) translate to the ~5-fold sensitivity difference (C17). The interpretation (C15) correctly follows from the model definition. This finding replicates across subjects and measurement sets.

results.result: Within V1, there is little to no systematic change in chromatic sensitivity (ellipse angle or minor axis ratio) as a function of eccentricity from 0° to 20°, though parameter variability exists at each eccentricity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C32 are supported by cortical surface maps (Figure 8) and scatter plots (Figure 9, Tables 1-2) showing minimal systematic variation in QCM parameters with eccentricity. While C34 notes that changes from 0° to 20° are small compared to vertical spread, and some parameter changes exceed measurement-to-measurement variability (Tables 1-2), the overall conclusion of little systematic change is justified. Outside V1, lower R² and higher variability (C33) appropriately limit conclusions to V1.

results.result: V1 BOLD responses generally increase with contrast for each chromatic direction, but the rate of increase varies substantially with chromatic direction, requiring ~60% contrast in the 45° direction versus ~12% in the -45° direction to elicit similar responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are directly supported by contrast response functions in Figure 2 and supplements. The monotonic increase with contrast (C21) is expected and observed. The direction-dependent sensitivity (C22) is quantified by the specific example (C23) showing 5-fold difference in contrast requirements. This provides the empirical basis for the QCM's elliptical isoresponse contours.

results.result: The single Naka-Rushton nonlinearity of the QCM accurately captures the dependence of GLM beta weights on equivalent contrast across all chromatic directions without apparent bias, though stimuli did not drive responses into the saturated regime.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by Figure 7 showing GLM beta weights plotted against equivalent contrast with good agreement to the QCM nonlinearity across all chromatic directions. However, C31 notes an important limitation: the stimuli did not reach saturation, meaning the shape of the nonlinearity at high contrasts is not constrained. This limits conclusions about the precise form of the nonlinearity but supports the separability assumption of the QCM within the tested range.

results.result: The GLM achieved median R² values of 0.41 (Measurement Set 1) and 0.32 (Measurement Set 2) for Subject 2 when fitting V1 BOLD time courses.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 directly reports GLM fit quality metrics for Subject 2, supported by Figure 3. These R² values provide context for evaluating the QCM performance. The difference between measurement sets may reflect variation in data quality or other factors, but both values indicate meaningful stimulus-driven variance is captured.

results.result: An alternative Linear Channels Model (LCM) accounts for the data about as well as the QCM, with isoresponse contours that approximate but are not perfectly elliptical, while constraining the QCM ellipse angle to 0° results in noticeably lower cross-validated R².
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by Figure 4—supplement 1 and Figure 6—supplement 1. The LCM achieves similar cross-validated R² to the QCM (C100), with approximately elliptical but not perfect isoresponse contours (C101). The constrained QCM with angle locked to 0° shows noticeably lower R² (C102), demonstrating that the data have power to reject incorrect isoresponse contour shapes. This validates that the elliptical form is empirically supported, not just assumed.

results.result: The experimental design used spatially uniform (0 c.p.d.) chromatic temporal modulations at 12 Hz in 8 chromatic directions at 5 log-spaced contrast levels, presented in 12-second blocks to three subjects with normal color vision, who performed an attention task with 100% accuracy across 960 total blocks per subject.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19, C40-C42, C56-C68 provide a comprehensive description of the experimental design, stimuli, subjects, and task performance. These are methodological specifications directly stated in the Materials and Methods section. The 100% attention task performance (C67) confirms subjects maintained attention throughout. This establishes the experimental foundation for all results.

results.result: Stimuli were generated using a OneLight Spectra digital light synthesis device with 56 independent primaries, employing silent substitution to selectively modulate cone photoreceptors while accounting for eccentricity-dependent cone fundamentals and age-related lens density, with spectroradiometric validation before and after each session.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C55 describe the stimulus generation and calibration procedures. These are methodological details directly stated in Materials and Methods, with validation measurements provided in Tables 5-7. The approach to account for eccentricity-dependent cone fundamentals (C50-C51) is a methodological strength that distinguishes this study from prior work and is relevant to interpreting the eccentricity results.

results.result: MRI data were acquired using HCP LifeSpan protocol on a 3T Siemens Prisma, preprocessed using HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline with ICAFIX denoising, motion censoring (FD > 0.5), and polynomial detrending, with V1 ROI defined using neuropythy anatomical template (0-20° eccentricity), and models fit using leave-runs-out cross-validation with bootstrap error estimation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C95 comprehensively describe MRI acquisition, preprocessing, ROI definition, and analysis procedures. These are standard methodological details directly stated in Materials and Methods. The preprocessing steps (C75-C79) are appropriate for fMRI data. The cross-validation strategy (C88-C90) is properly designed to evaluate model performance. Code availability (C95) supports reproducibility.

results.result: Prior work establishes that psychophysical evidence supports cone-opponent (S-(L+M), L-M) and luminance (L+M) mechanisms, with physiological correlates in retinal ganglion cells and LGN, but studies have not converged on a widely accepted quantitative model of V1 chromatic response properties, partly due to considerable heterogeneity across individual neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 accurately summarize prior literature through appropriate citations. These claims establish the scientific context and motivation for developing the QCM. The citations support the statements about psychophysical mechanisms (C8), physiological evidence (C9), lack of consensus on V1 models (C10), and neuronal heterogeneity (C11). This provides appropriate background for the current work.

results.result: Prior fMRI work by Engel et al. (1997) found V1 BOLD signals maximally sensitive to L-M modulations at low temporal frequencies, with elliptical isoresponse contours similar to psychophysical isothreshold contours, though at higher temporal frequencies psychophysical contours shift to favor L+M sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 and C96-C97 accurately cite prior work by Engel et al. (1997) and related studies. These citations establish precedent for using elliptical isoresponse contours (C36) and provide context for the current findings. The temporal frequency dependence noted (C97) is relevant for interpreting the current results at 12 Hz. The citations appear accurate based on the descriptions provided.

results.result: Prior fMRI studies by Mullen et al. (2007) and Vanni et al. (2006) reported decreased V1 response to L-M modulations with eccentricity (attributed to random cone-ganglion cell connections), while D'Souza et al. (2016) found no change (supporting selective connections), differing from the current study's finding of no change in chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 accurately summarize prior fMRI studies and their interpretations. The comparison to the current results (C113) is appropriate. However, the evaluation notes important methodological differences between studies (stimulus properties, accounting for eccentricity-dependent cone fundamentals) that complicate direct comparison. The citations appear accurate and the discrepancies are acknowledged in the discussion.

results.result: Variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density can produce eccentricity-dependent deviations in cone contrast that prior studies did not account for, while the current study designed stimuli to produce the same contrasts in 2° and 15° cone fundamentals, with the lack of variation in chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity parsimoniously explained by retinal output that preserves chromatic sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 identify an important methodological consideration (eccentricity-dependent cone fundamentals) that distinguishes the current study from prior work. The current study's approach (C120) addresses this potential confound. However, the interpretation (C121) that retinal output preserves chromatic sensitivity is one possible explanation but not uniquely determined by the data, as acknowledged in the discussion. The claim is appropriately qualified as 'parsimonious' rather than definitive.

results.result: The QCM assumes that elliptical isoresponse contours maintain constant aspect ratio and orientation across response levels (only scale changes), with the minor axis corresponding to the most sensitive chromatic direction and the major axis to the least sensitive direction, parameterized by 6 free parameters total.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 and C12 describe fundamental assumptions and structure of the QCM model. These are definitional statements about the model as designed by the authors. The assumption of constant aspect ratio and orientation (C37) is a key constraint that makes the model tractable. The definitions of minor and major axes (C38-C39) follow from standard geometric interpretation. The 6-parameter structure (C12) is clearly specified.

results.result: A quadratic isoresponse contour can be produced by a quadratic mechanism computing the sum of squared responses of two underlying linear mechanisms, but the isoresponse contours do not uniquely determine the sensitivity of underlying linear mechanisms, even within the QCM framework.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 correctly describe theoretical considerations about the relationship between quadratic isoresponse contours and underlying mechanisms, with appropriate citation to Poirson et al. (1990). This acknowledges an important limitation: the QCM characterizes the aggregate response but does not uniquely identify the underlying neural mechanisms. This is an appropriate caveat for interpreting the model parameters.

results.result: The spatially uniform 12 Hz stimuli could drive 'color', 'luminance', and 'color-luminance' cells, with 0 c.p.d. stimuli presumably producing strong responses in color cells (low-pass spatial filters), and the ~5-fold L-M vs L+M sensitivity ratio matching the ratio of color cell vs luminance/color-luminance cell firing rates at low spatial frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 attempt to relate the QCM results to single-cell electrophysiology. While the comparison to firing rate ratios from Schluppeck and Engel (2002) analyzing Johnson et al. (2001) data is interesting (C105-C106), this connection is speculative. The inference about which cell types are driven (C103-C104) is reasonable but not directly tested. The 12 Hz temporal frequency may shift responses relative to the cited analysis. The aggregate BOLD response reflects a complex mixture of cell types, making direct comparisons uncertain.

results.result: The data do not distinguish whether V1 response properties are inherited from the LGN or shaped by V1 processing, though the stimuli would robustly drive LGN cells projecting to V1, and the measured sensitivities may be inherited from earlier stages or affected by cortical feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 appropriately acknowledge a fundamental limitation of the fMRI approach: spatial localization to V1 does not determine the processing stage responsible for the observed response properties. The inference that stimuli would drive LGN cells (C108) is reasonable based on stimulus properties and citation to Lankheet et al. (1998). results.result: Prior electrophysiology work by Horwitz and Hass (2012) found that roughly half of macaque V1 neurons were best fit by quadratic isoresponse surfaces (some ellipsoidal, some hyperbolic) while the other half were fit by linear models with parallel plane isoresponse surfaces.

results.result: Studies show random or close-to-random L- and M-cone inputs to midget ganglion cells in the periphery, though not all studies agree, and possible cortical compensation mechanisms include supra-threshold compensation (as postulated in contrast perception and anomalous trichromacy) or differential integration area changes, though the latter is not supported by pRF measurements.

results.result: The QCM could potentially be generalized to the full L-M-S cone contrast space using ellipsoidal isoresponse surfaces, to different temporal frequencies to examine sensitivity changes, and to different spatial frequencies to model responses to complex spatial stimuli, which would place constraints on forward models of BOLD response to chromatic modulations.

The connection to forward models of BOLD response (C131-C133) is appropriate, noting that how to generalize such models to chromatic modulations is currently unknown (C132). These are appropriately framed as speculation about future work rather than current findings.
